opus-5.5.text:
It's a great question, and I think about it a lot. Right now I'd actually like to see more observation. Not less theory, but more patient, careful looking at what these systems actually do.

There's a tendency in machine learning to jump straight to a hypothesis and a benchmark. You have an idea, you test it, you get a number, and you move on. That's valuable, but it skips a step that's been really important in the history of science: just looking. Natural history came before a lot of biology. People spent years drawing birds and cataloguing beetles before anyone had a theory of evolution to organize it all. I think we're in a similar spot with neural networks. We have these incredibly rich, strange objects, and we've barely started describing them.

Part of my bias comes from my background in visualization. Over and over, I've seen that when you simply make the internals of a model visible, you find things nobody predicted. The embedding has some odd geometric structure, or a neuron responds to a combination of features you'd never have guessed. Those surprises are where good theory comes from. If you only test the hypotheses you already have, you'll never stumble on the ones you didn't think to have.

So I'd love to see the field give more credit to careful descriptive work: "here's a phenomenon, here's exactly what it looks like, we don't fully understand it yet." That kind of paper can be hard to publish, because reviewers want a clean claim and a big result. But some of the most useful work in interpretability has been exactly that, people noticing something weird and documenting it well.

That said, I don't want to romanticize observation. Eventually you need theory to tell you which observations matter, and to make predictions you can check. What I'd hope for is a healthier loop between the two, where looking feeds theorizing and theorizing tells you where to look next. Right now I think the looking half is a bit underweighted, and we'd benefit from evening that out.

r001.rationale: The response says careful observation is underweighted and calls for more looking at what systems actually do relative to theorizing.

r002.rationale: It supports giving descriptive papers more credit even when phenomena are not fully understood, but does not clearly advocate that academic conferences welcome such papers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the pendulum has swung quite far toward theory in a certain sense, and in another sense toward pure engineering, and what's gotten squeezed out in the middle is careful observation. If you look at the history of science, almost every field had a long descriptive phase before it had a theoretical one. Astronomy had Tycho Brahe before it had Kepler, and Kepler before Newton. Biology had people cataloguing species and drawing cells for centuries before anything like a unifying theory arrived. We have this strange situation in AI where we've built objects that are genuinely complex, that we don't understand, and yet there's a kind of impatience about just looking at them.

So what I'd like to see is more legitimacy given to the descriptive, naturalistic work. Go into a model, poke at it, find something surprising, write it down carefully, even if you don't have a grand theory to explain it yet. I think there's been a bias in the field where if you can't wrap a result in a theorem or a benchmark number, it's treated as anecdote. But a lot of the most important things we've learned about neural networks started as anecdotes. Somebody noticed a weird phenomenon, and then the theory caught up later.

And I'd add that visualization and interactive tools are a big part of this for me. Observation isn't passive. The instruments you build determine what you can see. A good interface for exploring a model's internals is as much a scientific contribution as a new theorem, and I'd like the field's incentives to reflect that. So the change I'm hoping for isn't that theory goes away, it's that we stop treating observation as the thing you do before the real work starts, and recognize it as the real work.

r001.rationale: The response says the pendulum has swung far toward theory and that careful observation has been squeezed out of AI research.

r002.rationale: It advocates giving descriptive work more legitimacy, including without a grand theory, but does not specifically say academic conferences should welcome such papers.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see more careful observation, and more respect for it as a contribution. We have these systems that do surprising things, and often we’re better at building them than we are at explaining what they’re doing. That seems like a good moment to slow down and look closely.

My background is in visualization, so I’m naturally interested in tools that let you notice something you weren’t expecting. A good observation can give you a new question, or show you that the question you were asking wasn’t quite right.

And then you need theory to make sense of what you’ve seen and generate predictions you can test. I’d like a tighter loop between those activities: observe, form an explanation, test it, and look again. There’s a lot of scientific value in simply establishing, carefully, what’s happening.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls for more careful observation and respect for it, but does not say AI research currently overemphasizes theory relative to observation.

r002.rationale: It values careful observation as scientifically useful, but does not mention academic conferences or welcoming papers without explanations.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see observation get more respect. There’s a tendency to think that the real contribution has to be a new algorithm or a theorem, and that simply looking carefully at what a model does is somehow less scientific. But careful observation is often where science starts. You notice something surprising, you work out whether it’s a real phenomenon, and then you try to explain it.

That seems especially important in AI, where we can build systems whose behavior we don’t fully understand. I’d love to see more work that says, “Here’s an interesting thing this system does, here are the conditions under which it happens, and here’s what we still don’t understand.” Theory and observation should feed each other. We need room for the observations that give us better questions to theorize about.

r001.rationale: The response says observation deserves more respect and contrasts it with the tendency to value new algorithms or theorems as the real contribution.

r002.rationale: It supports reporting observations and unresolved questions, but does not say academic conferences should welcome purely observational papers without explanations.
